evidence: ProjectController.create, UserController.create and TaskController.create/listByProject/assign/complete all parse input with `new RequestParser(req.<source>, '<Label>')` and its requiredString/optionalString methods
Every handler in ProjectController.ts, TaskController.ts and UserController.ts passes errors to `next(error)` and contains no local error mapping
Validation logic stays inside the use cases: TaskController.create passes the optional `status` and `dueDate` strings to CreateTaskUseCase.execute without checking them itself

TaskController.ts declares `TaskUseCases`, which groups CreateTaskUseCase, ListProjectTasksUseCase, AssignTaskUseCase and CompleteTaskUseCase; ProjectController and UserController each inject a single use case
Each controller handles only its own resource: ProjectController (projects), TaskController (tasks), UserController (users)
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The unit passes. All three files share one concern: Express HTTP controllers that turn requests into application use-case calls. Every handler parses input through the module's RequestParser abstraction. None reads req.body, req.params or req.query fields directly. Each handler sends errors to next(error) instead of mapping them itself, so error handling stays in one place, outside the controllers. No domain rule or invariant is repeated across the files. Each controller handles one resource (projects, tasks, users). Two minor points don't count as violations. First, the try/catch/next boilerplate repeats in every handler, but it's a pattern, not a duplicated rule. Second, TaskController receives its use cases as one TaskUseCases object, while the other two receive a single use case. With four use cases, grouping them is reasonable and doesn't bypass any abstraction.
